en: Sutta Nipāta 4.11 Kalahavivādasutta:
"From what do quarrels and disputes arise?"
Lamentation and sorrow, along with stinginess;
pride and arrogance, together with slander—whence have these arisen? Pray, tell me that.
“Abundant affection brings quarrels and disputes,
along with lamentation, sorrow, and envy;
as well as pride, arrogance, and slander.”
“From stinginess arise quarrels and disputes;
from those born of dispute come slanders.
From what source, then, do dear things in this world arise?”
And those cravings that wander about the world,
as well as the hopes and ends that lead a man to his future state— wherefrom do they originate?
“Desire is the cause of what is dear in the world,
as well as those cravings that roam the world through greed;
both hope and its fulfillment have their origin in this.”
“Which things lead a man to the future life?
“From what source does desire arise in the world,
and from what are decisions brought forth?”
Anger, false speech, and doubt,
or whatever other states have been described by the ascetic:
"That which is called 'pleasant' and 'unpleasant' in the world..."
Depending upon that, desire arises;
having seen both dissolution and origination among forms,
a person in the world makes a judgment.
Anger, false speech, and doubt—
even these phenomena, though they appear as pairs, exist only as such.
One who is full of doubt should train in the path of knowledge.
“Having understood the teachings proclaimed by the ascetic:
‘From what source do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise?
In the absence of what do these not come to be?’”
"Tell me this matter, from what source it arises: both non-existence and existence.
"Pleasant and unpleasant [feeling] have contact as their source."
When contact is absent, these do not come to be;
both non-existence and existence—
this matter I declare to you has its source from this.
“From what cause does contact arise in the world?
And from what are possessions brought forth?
When what is absent is there no sense of ‘mine’?”
“When what has vanished do contacts no longer touch?
“Contact depends upon name-and-form;
possessions have craving as their source.”
"When desire has been abandoned, there is no 'mine-ness';
when form has vanished, contacts do not touch.
"How does form vanish for one who is composed?"
"How does both pleasure and pain cease?
Tell me this, how it ceases;
such was the thought in my mind: 'May I understand that.'"
“Neither perceiving perception, nor perceiving non-perception,
nor being non-percipient, nor having perception extinguished—
for one who is thus composed, form disappears.”
"For conceptual proliferation has its source in perception.
"What we asked you, you have explained to us;
now we ask another thing—please tell us that."
"Some wise ones here say that purification for a *yakkha* consists only of this much;
or do they say there is something else beyond this?"
“Some wise ones here say that purity for a yakkha consists of this much;
yet others speak of a different doctrine for them.”
Those skilled in speech declare that there is no residue remaining.
Having understood that these [defilements] are dependent,
the sage, having known them, investigates their bases.
"Knowing this, the liberated one does not enter into dispute;
the wise one does not strive for existence after existence.
Thus ends the eleventh discourse, the *Kalahavivāda-sutta*.
